system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2148-03-26 19:54:00 to 2148-04-04 12:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with a dislodged nephrostomy tube, left flank pain, and signs of kidney infection. Imaging confirmed severe left hydroureteronephrosis due to tube dysfunction. He underwent successful nephrostomy tube exchange with secure fixation. He was treated with IV meropenem for pyelonephritis, though he declined the final IV dose and oral antibiotic initiation in the hospital. He was discharged with a prescription for oral fosfomycin to complete the course. His chronic left hip wound was monitored, and leg swelling was evaluated, revealing a subacute tibial fracture without need for intervention. Renal function remained stable, and he was discharged home with follow-up instructions for urology, orthopedics, and medication adherence.
problems: Infection of incontinent external stoma of urinary tract
Pressure ulcer of left hip, stage 4
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease with stage 1 through stage 4 chronic kidney disease, or unspecified chronic kidney disease
Other fracture of upper end of left tibia, subsequent encounter for closed fracture with routine healing

procedure.

100mcg of fentanyl throughout the total intra-service time of 9 min during
which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored by an
independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and
subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: As above
CONTRAST: 5 ml of Optiray contrast.

PROCEDURE:
1. Limited contrast injection of existing left PCN
2. Left 8 ___ nephrostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient.The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed prone
on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol. 
The left flank was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Diluted contrast was injected into the left nephrostomy to confirm catheter
position. The image was stored on PACS. Local anesthesia was administered with
instillation of lidocaine jelly and 1% subcutaneous lidocaine injection. The
catheter was cut.  A Roadrunner wire was advanced into the left nephrostomy
tube and advanced into the proximal ureter. The stay sutures were cut and the
catheter was removed over the wire. A new 10 ___ nephrostomy catheter was
flushed and advanced with its plastic stiffener over the wire into appropriate
position. The wire and stiffener were removed and the pigtail was formed. The
final image was saved. The catheter was secured with a Stat Lock device and
sterile dressings.  The catheter was attached to a bag for drainage.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
post-procedure complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because of left flank pain, fevers, and your nephrostomy tube isn’t draining well. We did a quick ultrasound in the ER and saw that your left kidney is very swollen. We’re concerned this is due to a blockage in your PCN tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been hurting more than usual. The tube’s been draining less, and I’ve felt feverish. Is that why my kidney’s swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tube is supposed to drain urine from your kidney, but it looks blocked. That’s causing pressure and infection. We’ve scheduled a procedure to replace it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had this before. But this time it feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white blood cell count is elevated, and your urine from the tube was cloudy. That suggests a significant infection. We’ll start IV antibiotics once the tube is replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Will they interact?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your list. You’re on meropenem, which is safe given your allergies. We’ll adjust doses for your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the PCN tube exchange this morning. It went well. The old tube was clogged and partially pulled out. We placed a new one, and 250 cc of cloudy fluid drained out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. Was it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we sent it for culture. In the meantime, you’re on IV meropenem to treat the infection. Your pain should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still hurting pretty bad. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered IV Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. We’ll monitor your intake since you’re not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function is stable—creatinine is 4.1, which is your baseline. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want it getting worse. What about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on culture results. For now, meropenem is covering the likely bacteria. We’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound yesterday. No abscess, and the left kidney isn’t hydronephrotic anymore. That means the new tube is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw your kidneys are echogenic, which fits with your chronic kidney disease. Nothing new there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture from your PCN fluid came back. It grew Staphylococcus aureus, but it’s methicillin-sensitive, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s treatable. We’re switching from meropenem to IV daptomycin, which works well for this bug. You’ll need a 14-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fourteen days? I’ll have to stay here that long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ideally, yes. We can arrange a PICC line so you can get antibiotics at home, or go to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want a PICC. I’ve had infections before. And I can’t go to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But stopping early could lead to relapse. We’ll discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is high—6.1. It’s something we watch with kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can affect your heart, but your EKG is normal. We’d like to give you kayexalate to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I can’t. It gives me terrible diarrhea, and I already struggle with bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll monitor it and recheck tomorrow. You should check it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures came back negative. That’s good—means the infection is likely localized to the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks like it. Your white count is coming down. But you’ve only had 5 days of daptomycin. You need 14.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I can’t stay. I’ll take it at home somehow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with urology. Your PCN is draining well. They’ll see you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my leg? It’s been aching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ortho reviewed your old fracture. You have a healing tibia fracture. They recommend follow-up, but no urgent action.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t gone yet. I’ll try to make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on day 7 of antibiotics. Your creatinine is stable at 3.9, and potassium is 6.0—still high but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better, but still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Infection takes a toll. We’re planning to taper your IV pain meds and switch back to your oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need those for pain. Don’t stop them too fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. But we need to prepare for discharge. We’re concerned about finishing the antibiotic course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll manage it. I don’t want to stay longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is day 8 of antibiotics. We’ve discussed options: home health, outpatient infusion, or stopping early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want any of those. I’ll take my chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We strongly advise completing the course. Incomplete treatment could lead to relapse or resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I’m leaving. I’ve been here too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll document your decision. Please follow up with urology, nephrology, and check your potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I know I need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been informed you’re planning to leave. We want to make sure you know the risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve made up my mind. I’m not staying for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your PCN is working, pain is better, and labs are stable. But you’ve only had 8 of 14 antibiotic days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll rest at home. I’ll call if I get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And follow up with your doctors. Your urine test also showed cocaine. We’re concerned about your use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I lost a close friend. I’ve been struggling. I slipped back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sorry to hear that. We’ve connected you with counseling resources. Please consider reaching out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I know I need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’ll send your records to your providers. Please come back if you develop fever, pain, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you were supposed to be discharged this morning, but we’ve been informed you left the hospital last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had to go. I couldn’t stay any longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand, but it’s important you follow up. Your infection isn’t fully treated, and your potassium is still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll call urology. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And consider speaking with someone about your loss and substance use. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your discharge plan. You eloped before formal discharge, but we’re documenting your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just needed to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. Just remember: finish your follow-ups, check your potassium, and call if you’re not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not either. Take care of yourself, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your PCN is functioning, infection markers improved, but antibiotic course incomplete. Follow-up critical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the calls today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your meds list and records. Please stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve finalized your discharge. You’ve completed 8 of 14 antibiotic days. Please follow up as discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Stay safe, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your elopement. Please contact us if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want this to happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. Take care of yourself, Mr. ___.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with left flank pain, fevers, and decreased output from his left nephrostomy tube, found to be occluded. He underwent successful PCN tube exchange with drainage of infected fluid. Cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, and he was started on IV daptomycin for a planned 14-day course. His chronic kidney disease remained stable, but he developed hyperkalemia (K 6.1), which he declined treatment for. He also acknowledged recent cocaine use related to grief over a friend’s death. Despite medical advice, he eloped on hospital day 8, having completed only part of his antibiotic course. He was alert and stable at the time, with functioning PCN and improved pain, but was strongly advised to follow up with urology, nephrology, and outpatient support.
